title: AML Agents Briefing — Thursday, 03 September 2026
script:
ALEX: Welcome to AML Agents Briefing. It's Thursday, the third of September 2026. I'm Alex, joined as always by Jordan. This is your audio overview of the most material AML and financial crime developments across the Asia-Pacific region today. Full detail, the obligation register, and horizon scanning are all at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: Big day, Alex. We've got a ransomware attack with real compliance consequences, a shifting landscape for alternative data in credit, and a clutch of obligations that are closer than some listeners probably realise.

ALEX: Let's start with the story that has the most immediate operational relevance. Jack Henry and Associates, the Missouri-based core banking and payments technology provider serving around eight thousand US financial institutions, has confirmed a ransomware attack that disrupted its infrastructure. Now, Jack Henry isn't a household name in the Asia-Pacific, but if your group has US correspondent banking relationships, or if your technology stack touches any Jack Henry-connected counterparty, this matters to you.

JORDAN: Alex, what's the direct AML read-across here? Ransomware is an IT incident, but why should an MLRO be paying attention this morning?

ALEX: Two reasons. First, if transaction monitoring feeds, SAR filing systems, or sanctions screening rely on infrastructure connected to an affected Jack Henry client, you could have a gap in your AML controls you don't yet know about. Second, ransomware payments themselves frequently involve virtual assets and layering through multiple jurisdictions. The attack is both a disruption risk and a typology signal.

JORDAN: So the action here is straightforward. If you have US correspondent relationships, contact those counterparts today and ask specifically whether their core banking or payments infrastructure runs on Jack Henry systems. Document the response. If there's any dependency, escalate to your group head of financial crime before the end of the week and review your business-continuity obligations under your AML programme. For AML/CTF compliance officers in Australia, that's a live obligation under the AML/CTF Act.

ALEX: Shifting focus, Block has announced it will commercialise Cash App Score, the proprietary credit signal derived from real-time transaction flows across its fifty-seven-million-user payments network, making it available to other lenders. This is a substantive development for anyone thinking about alternative data in credit underwriting.

JORDAN: And the compliance question here is about what regulators in this region will make of it. If a lender in Hong Kong or Singapore starts incorporating a signal derived from a US payments platform into its credit decisioning, what does that mean for know-your-customer governance and explainability?

ALEX: Exactly. The Monetary Authority of Singapore's Notice 626 on technology risk and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's guidance on model risk both require that institutions understand and can explain the inputs to credit models. A black-box score from a third-party payments network raises immediate questions about model governance and fair lending.

JORDAN: If you're the head of financial crime compliance or the chief risk officer at a digital bank or an electronic money institution in the region, add this to your model risk committee agenda now. Before your institution signs any data-sharing arrangement with an alternative data provider, verify that your model governance framework covers third-party-derived signals, and confirm your customer disclosures are adequate. That's a gap that supervisors will find quickly.

ALEX: Now, a quick note on obligations. Jordan, you want to take this one?

JORDAN: Yes. Three deadlines are worth flagging this week. For listeners in Hong Kong, the HKMA self-assessment return covering the calendar year 2024 period is due by the thirtieth of September, submitted via the HKMA-prescribed Excel template with internal audit validation required. That is four weeks away. If you haven't started, start today. For AUSTRAC-regulated entities in Australia, your calendar year 2024 annual compliance report should already be lodged. If it isn't, daily civil penalties are accruing and a misleading attestation carries criminal liability under section 137 of the relevant legislation. And for Indonesia, the annual independent review of your AML and CFT programme covering calendar year 2024 should have gone to your Risk Oversight Committee and Board of Commissioners by June. If there's a gap in your documentation trail, address it now.

ALEX: Moving to what to watch. AUSTRAC has issued a forty-seven million Australian dollar civil penalty against a major registered digital currency exchange for systemic failures in transaction monitoring, mule-account detection, and suspicious matter report timeliness. That enforcement action caps a twelve-month investigation and is the clearest signal yet of where AUSTRAC's supervisory focus sits for the digital asset sector.

JORDAN: The read-across for any AUSTRAC-registered digital currency exchange is direct. Pull your last six months of suspicious matter report metrics this week. Look at timeliness, look at your mule-account detection rules, and stress-test whether your transaction monitoring configuration would catch the patterns AUSTRAC cited. If you're preparing for a supervisory review, that's where the examiner will start. And with Tranche 2 guidance for legal practitioners already published, if you advise or work with law firms coming into scope, now is the time to map their customer-engagement triggers and source-of-wealth obligations before they come to you asking.

JORDAN: That's your briefing for the third of September. Full detail on every story, the complete obligation register, and our horizon-scanning feed are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. It's free, it's updated daily, and it's built for practitioners.

ALEX: Thanks for listening. We'll be back tomorrow. Stay sharp.
